# Course Syllabus and Week Map {#sec-syllabus}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Appendix status: drafted.** A mapping from the book's thirty-nine chapters
onto a fourteen-week semester, plus shorter paths for readers who are not
taking the course.
:::

The book is deliberately larger than one semester. This appendix answers "which
chapters do I actually have to read, and in what order?"

[Thirty-nine chapters do not fit in fourteen weeks, and pretending otherwise
produces a course that covers everything badly.]{.hl} What follows assigns
about two chapters a week, names what gets cut, and says plainly that the cut
material is reference rather than an oversight.

## The fourteen-week course {#sec-syllabus-weeks}

| wk | chapters | in class | due |
|--:|:--|:--|:--|
| 1 | @sec-why-nlp, @sec-text-as-data | Tokenize Turkish and English side by side; count what breaks | — |
| 2 | @sec-embeddings, @sec-bake-off | Run the bake-off; argue about the baseline | Lab 1 |
| 3 | @sec-data-annotation | Annotate 50 items in pairs; measure disagreement | — |
| 4 | @sec-language-models, @sec-transformers | Attention by hand on one sentence | Lab 2 |
| 5 | @sec-pretraining, @sec-post-training | Fertility on your own text; convert to cost | **Capstone proposal** |
| 6 | @sec-classification, @sec-sequence-labeling | Fine-tune one encoder; read the errors | Lab 3 |
| 7 | @sec-turkish-nlp | The control-measurement workshop | — |
| 8 | @sec-prompting, @sec-decoding | Structured output, and making it fail | **Capstone eval set** |
| 9 | @sec-retrieval, @sec-rag | Build retrieval; measure it *alone* | Lab 4 |
| 10 | @sec-llm-eval | Audit a judge; size an eval set | — |
| 11 | @sec-agent-anatomy, @sec-tool-design | Build the smallest agent that works | **Mid-point check-in** |
| 12 | @sec-context-engineering, @sec-agent-eval | Trajectory versus outcome scoring | Lab 5 |
| 13 | @sec-agent-security, @sec-guardrails | Attack each other's agents | — |
| 14 | @sec-capstone | Demos | **Capstone due** |

: A fourteen-week path through the book {tbl-colwidths="[6,30,40,24]"}

Three deliberate choices in that table, each of which someone will disagree
with.

**Week 7 is spent on Turkish alone.** For a course taught at a Turkish
university it is the highest-value week in the semester, and
@sec-turkish-nlp-pattern's pattern — standard tools silently wrong outside
English — is a lesson that transfers to every other topic.

**Evaluation arrives at week 10, before agents.** @sec-llm-eval has to precede
@sec-agent-eval or students build agents they cannot assess. The capstone's
eval-set deadline at week 8 is earlier still, deliberately.

**Week 13 is adversarial and hands-on.** Students attack each other's agents.
Reading @sec-agent-security convinces nobody; a planted instruction that works
on the first try convinces everybody.

## What gets cut, and why that is fine {#sec-syllabus-cut}

Fifteen chapters are not on the list — twenty-four assigned, fifteen cut,
thirty-nine in total. They are not lesser material, and several are the most
immediately useful chapters in the book for someone already working. They are
cut because a semester is short.

| cut | chapters | who should read it anyway |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Most of Part VI** | @sec-serving, @sec-gateway, @sec-deployment, @sec-observability, @sec-production-eval, @sec-governance | Anyone who will operate a system rather than build a prototype. This is the usual casualty and the most reference-like part of the book. |
| **Advanced agents** | @sec-memory, @sec-mcp, @sec-multi-agent, @sec-agentic-rag | Students whose capstone needs them; read on demand |
| **Adjacent tasks** | @sec-clustering, @sec-summarization, @sec-machine-translation, @sec-multimodal | Read the one your problem is |
| **Depth** | @sec-reasoning | After the course, when the rest has settled |

: What a fourteen-week course leaves out {tbl-colwidths="[18,40,42]"}

Part VI being the casualty is worth saying plainly rather than hiding: a course
can teach you to build something that works once, and Part VI is about the
difference between that and something that keeps working. Students who go
straight into industry should read it first, in that order.

## Three shorter paths {#sec-syllabus-paths}

**(a) The practitioner who only wants agents.** Start at @sec-agent-anatomy and
read Part V, then @sec-agent-eval, @sec-agent-security and @sec-guardrails.
Detour back to @sec-prompting and @sec-decoding when structured output stops
behaving, and to @sec-rag when retrieval does. Roughly ten chapters.

**(b) The statistician who wants the modelling story.** Parts I–III in order —
@sec-why-nlp through @sec-turkish-nlp — then jump to @sec-llm-eval, which is
the chapter this book was most obviously written for a statistician. Then
@sec-agent-eval and @sec-production-eval for how the same reasoning survives
contact with production.

**(c) The reader who wants Turkish NLP specifically.** @sec-text-as-data →
@sec-bake-off → @sec-turkish-nlp, then the Turkish measurements embedded
elsewhere: @sec-sequence-labeling's contamination finding,
@sec-summarization's ROUGE tokenizer bug, and @sec-machine-translation's
metric asymmetry. @sec-turkish-resources is the catalogue.

## Assessment and course policies {#sec-syllabus-assessment}

The table above is a reading map; this is the part that makes it a syllabus.
Weights are a starting point for whoever teaches from this, not a rule — but
having *no* weights is the failure mode, because students allocate effort to
what is graded and a course that will not say what that is has already chosen
for them.

| component | weight | when |
|:--|--:|:--|
| Five labs, submitted as notebooks | 25% (5% each) | weeks 2, 4, 6, 9, 12 |
| Capstone proposal | pass/fail gate | week 5 |
| Capstone eval set | 5% | week 8 |
| Mid-point go/no-go review | 5% | week 11 |
| Participation in the week-13 adversarial session | 10% | week 13 |
| Capstone repository, report and demo | 55% | week 14 |

: A suggested grading scheme {tbl-colwidths="[46,20,34]"}

**There is no written exam**, and the reason is the argument of the book.
[A number you cannot defend is worthless, and a three-hour exam cannot test
whether you can defend one.]{.hl} What replaces it is the ten-minute oral check
inside the demo, where every team member answers questions about any part of
the submission — which is a harder examination of understanding than a paper is,
and a fairer one for students who build well and write slowly.

**Labs** are due at the end of the week they belong to, and the lowest score is
dropped: one bad week should not follow a student through a semester.

**The three capstone gates cannot be made up.** They exist to stop a project
failing at week 13, and a late gate has already failed at that job. Late
policy on the final submission is the instructor's to set — announce it in
week 1 rather than in week 14.

**Week 13 is the one session that cannot be replicated asynchronously**,
because students attack *each other's* agents and there is nothing to attack
alone. Everything else can be caught up from the book.

**Academic integrity, including LLM use**, is governed by
@sec-capstone-brief-integrity and applies to the labs as well as to the
capstone. Accessibility arrangements go through the university's disability
support unit and never require disclosing a diagnosis to the instructor.

## Prerequisites {#sec-syllabus-prereq}

Concretely, what you should be able to do in week 1 — not what you should have
taken.

**Required.** Read and modify a Python script of a hundred lines. Work with
lists, dictionaries and files. Read a table of numbers and say what it means.
Have installed something with `pip` and had it fail.

**Assumed but refreshable.** Vectors and dot products, conditional probability,
and what "minimising a loss" means. @sec-math-refresher covers each in two
lines with a pointer to where the book uses it; read it in week 1 rather than
when you are stuck.

**Explicitly not required.** Deep-learning coursework, GPU access, calculus
beyond derivatives-as-slopes, or prior NLP. The measurements in this book were
all run on one laptop, and @sec-setup is what you need to reproduce them.

**Not negotiable, and not technical.** Willingness to report a number that
disagrees with what you hoped. The book asks for that on nearly every page, and
the capstone rubric in @sec-capstone-brief grades it.
